In [D16](D16-dam-nutrient-impact-foodweb.qmd), poor water quality brought
slightly more species, and in [D17](D17-pressure-traits.qmd)
the species lost with each pressure shared traits (cold-water,
flowing-water, intolerant species). A gain of species can thus hide a loss
of functions, if the species gained are functionally similar and those lost
are specialists [REF: Mouillot et al. 2013, doi:10.1016/j.tree.2012.10.004]
[REF: Villéger et al. 2010, doi:10.1890/09-1310.1]. Here we measure the
functional diversity of each community and ask whether it decreases with the
pressures at equal species richness.

Steps: (1) choose the traits, (2) build a functional space, (3) measure the
functional richness and dispersion of each community and compare them with a
null model at equal richness, (4) relate them to dams and water quality.

## Setup

```{r setup}
library(renv)
renv::load()
library(targets)
library(here)
tar_config_set(
  store = here::here("_targets")
)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
devtools::load_all()
nice_theme()
```

```{r palette}
colour_group <- c(
  Diet = "#009E73", Habitat = "#0072B2", `Size and life history` = "#E69F00",
  Reproduction = "#CC79A7", Morphology = "#56B4E9"
)
colour_effect <- c(Positive = "#2166AC", `Not credible` = "grey70", Negative = "#B2182B")
pressure_label <- c(
  ammonium = "Ammonium", orthophosphate = "Orthophosphate",
  oxygen_saturation = "Oxygen saturation", temperature = "Water temperature",
  accumulation = "Dams to the sea", dam_below = "Dam just downstream",
  dam_above = "Dam just upstream"
)
# Terms of the D18 models: phosphorus and oxygen are left out, as part of the
# same pollution syndrome as ammonium.
model_label <- pressure_label[c("ammonium", "temperature", "accumulation", "dam_below", "dam_above")]
```

## Traits

Functional diversity should describe what species do in the ecosystem
("effect traits": diet, habitat use, size, reproduction, morphology) rather
than how they respond to pressures ("response traits", e.g. tolerances)
[REF: Lavorel & Garnier 2002, doi:10.1046/j.1365-2435.2002.00664.x]
[REF: Villéger et al. 2017, Hydrobiologia, doi to check]. We select the
traits of the Dézerald et al. table (D17) with four rules:

1. **Effect traits only.** The tolerances (to water quality, oxygen,
   temperature, habitat degradation) and the obstacle crossing classes are
   excluded: they define how species respond to the pressures tested below,
   so including them would make the test partly circular.
2. **Complete:** known for at least 90% of the species. This drops growth
   rates, body sizes other than the maximum, migration distances, egg size,
   upper thermal tolerance, number of reproductive cycles, relative fecundity
   and respiration.
3. **Not redundant:** maximum length rather than maximum weight; the fuzzy
   diet rather than the feeding guild summarising it; the morphological
   ratios rather than body shape and swimming mode. Migration is left out as
   the trait of the dam hypotheses in D17.
4. **Equal weight per group of traits:** the distance between species is the
   mean of the distances of five groups, so that the nine morphological
   ratios do not outweigh the rest
   [REF: de Bello et al. 2021, doi:10.1111/2041-210X.13537].

```{r trait}
variable <- tar_read(functional_variable)
metadata <- tar_read(dezerald_metadata) |>
  distinct(trait, name)
variable |>
  mutate(
    Description = case_when(
      variable == "diet" ~ "Diet: affinity to detritus, plants and animals of three sizes (proportions)",
      variable == "living" ~ "Vertical position: bottom, near bottom, open water (fuzzy)",
      variable == "hab.RHEO" ~ "Rheophily, from still to flowing water (5 classes)",
      variable == "hab.TROPH" ~ "Feeding position: bottom or water column",
      variable == "life.LONG" ~ "Longevity",
      .default = metadata$name[match(variable, metadata$trait)]
    ),
    type = c(fuzzy = "Fuzzy", ordinal = "Ordered classes", nominal = "Categories")[type]
  ) |>
  select(Group = group, Trait = variable, Description, Type = type) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Each trait gives a distance in [0, 1] between two species (categories: 0 if
same, 1 otherwise; ordered classes: difference over the range; fuzzy: half
the sum of the absolute differences of affinities), averaged within groups
then across groups. Missing values are ignored pair by pair (target
`functional_distance`).

```{r trait-group}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between the distance of each trait group and the overall distance between species."

distance <- tar_read(functional_distance)
lower <- lower.tri(distance$distance)
tibble(
  group = dimnames(distance$group)[[3]],
  r = apply(distance$group, 3, \(g) cor(g[lower], distance$distance[lower]))
) |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, rev(names(colour_group)))) |>
  ggplot(aes(r, group, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = colour_group) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = "Correlation with the overall distance", y = NULL) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

**Results:**

- All five groups contribute to the overall distance, reproduction the most
  and morphology the least.

## Functional space

The species are placed in a space whose axes are those of a principal
coordinate analysis of the distance. The number of axes is chosen by how
well the distances in the space match the original distances (mean absolute
deviation) [REF: Maire et al. 2015, doi:10.1111/geb.12299], using mFD
[REF: Magneville et al. 2022, doi:10.1111/ecog.05904].

```{r space-quality}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Quality of the functional space: mean absolute deviation between the distances in the space and the trait distances (lower is better)."

space <- tar_read(functional_space)
axis_number <- tar_read(functional_axis_number)
space$quality_fspaces |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("space") |>
  mutate(axes = as.integer(sub("pcoa_(\\d+)d", "\\1", space))) |>
  ggplot(aes(axes, mad)) +
  geom_line(color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(color = axes == axis_number), size = 2.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#B2182B", `FALSE` = "grey30")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(x = "Number of axes", y = "Mean absolute deviation")
```

```{r space}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "Species in the functional space (first four axes). Arrows: correlation of selected traits with the axes."

coord <- tar_read(functional_coord)
trait <- tar_read(functional_trait)
species_coord <- as_tibble(coord, rownames = "species")
loading_trait <- c(
  "Rheophily" = "hab.RHEO", "Maximum length" = "morp.LMAX", "Longevity" = "life.LONG",
  "Large prey" = "diet.ANI9", "Plants" = "diet.PLANT4", "Detritus" = "diet.DET1",
  "Bottom-dwelling" = "living.BENT", "Open water" = "living.PEL", "Elongated body" = "morp.BLBD"
)
loading <- cor(coord, trait[match(rownames(coord), trait$species), loading_trait], use = "pairwise") |>
  t() |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(trait = names(loading_trait))
plot_plane <- function(x, y) {
  scale <- 0.8 * max(abs(coord[, c(x, y)]))
  ggplot(species_coord, aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]])) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = scale * .data[[x]], yend = scale * .data[[y]]),
      data = loading, color = "#B2182B", linewidth = 0.4,
      arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.15, "cm"))
    ) +
    geom_point(color = "grey30", size = 1.3) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
      aes(label = species), size = 2.1, fontface = "italic", color = "grey45",
      max.overlaps = 6, segment.size = 0.2, seed = 1
    ) +
    ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
      aes(scale * .data[[x]], scale * .data[[y]], label = trait),
      data = loading, color = "#B2182B", size = 2.8, fontface = "bold",
      label.size = NA, fill = alpha("white", 0.8), min.segment.length = Inf, seed = 1
    ) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = sub("PC", "Axis ", x), y = sub("PC", "Axis ", y)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(plot_plane("PC1", "PC2"), plot_plane("PC3", "PC4"))
```

**Results:**

- Four axes represent the distances well (mean absolute deviation 0.06,
  below the usual threshold of 0.1).
- Axis 1 runs from small still-water species (mosquitofish, stickleback,
  bitterling) to large, long-lived, flowing-water and migratory species
  (salmon, barbel, lampreys).
- Axis 2 runs from bottom-dwellers (sculpin, brook lamprey, stone loach) to
  open-water predators (pike, largemouth bass, rudd).
- Axes 3 and 4 separate large-prey eaters from plant and detritus eaters.

## Functional diversity of the communities

Two indices are computed at each visit (target `functional_diversity`), on
presence (each species counts once):

- **functional richness**: the volume of the space filled by the species of
  the community, relative to the volume of all species
  [REF: Villéger et al. 2008, doi:10.1890/07-1206.1]; it needs more species
  than axes, so visits with `r axis_number` species or fewer are left out;
- **functional dispersion**: the mean distance of the species to the centre
  of the community [REF: Laliberté & Legendre 2010, doi:10.1890/08-2244.1],
  defined for any number of species.

Both increase with the number of species. To compare communities at equal
richness, the observed index is compared with 199 communities with the same
species but with the traits shuffled among species (target `functional_null`),
which keeps the richness of each community and the frequency of each
species. The standardised effect size (SES) is the observed value minus the
mean of the null values, divided by their standard deviation: negative when
the species are functionally more similar than expected by chance
[REF: Mouchet et al. 2010, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2435.2010.01695.x].

```{r diversity}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Functional richness and dispersion against species richness (top), and their standardised effect sizes (bottom). Lines: median per number of species."

ses <- tar_read(functional_ses)
index_label <- c(
  fric = "Functional richness", fdis = "Functional dispersion",
  fric_ses = "Functional richness (SES)", fdis_ses = "Functional dispersion (SES)"
)
ses |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(all_of(names(index_label)), names_to = "index") |>
  filter(is.finite(value)) |>
  mutate(index = factor(index_label[index], index_label)) |>
  ggplot(aes(richness, value)) +
  geom_hline(
    aes(yintercept = y), data = tibble(index = factor(index_label[3:4], index_label), y = 0),
    color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0, size = 0.4, alpha = 0.25, color = "#2166AC") +
  stat_summary(fun = median, geom = "line", color = "grey15", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~index, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Number of species", y = NULL)
```

```{r diversity-summary}
ses |>
  summarise(
    across(c(fric_ses, fdis_ses), list(
      visits = \(x) sum(is.finite(x)),
      median = \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
      below = \(x) mean(x < -1.96, na.rm = TRUE),
      above = \(x) mean(x > 1.96, na.rm = TRUE)
    ))
  ) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("index", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.*_ses)_(.*)") |>
  transmute(
    Index = index_label[index], Visits = visits, `Median SES` = round(median, 2),
    `Lower than chance` = scales::percent(below, 1), `Higher than chance` = scales::percent(above, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**Results:**

- Functional richness rises almost linearly with the number of species;
  functional dispersion saturates above about 8 species.
- At equal richness, most communities are slightly less diverse than
  expected by chance (median SES about −0.6): species that co-occur tend to
  share traits, as expected from environmental filtering.
- Few communities depart strongly from chance (SES beyond ±1.96).

## Dams, water quality and functional diversity

The SES of each index is modelled as the presence of species in D17
(Gaussian, same river position, sampling, site, year and spatial effects),
with the three dam metrics, yearly ammonium and water temperature (target
`functional_model`). Phosphorus and oxygen are left out of all the models
of this notebook: they belong to the same pollution syndrome as ammonium
(correlations 0.73 and −0.49), so controlling for them would remove part of
the effect of pollution. Temperature is kept as a natural gradient along
the river with its own effect on the fauna (D17). The ammonium effect is
thus the effect of the pollution syndrome it marks. The raw indices are
fitted too, for comparison.

```{r model}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| fig-cap: "Effect of dams and pressures on functional diversity (per standard deviation of the pressure, 91% credible interval). Left: raw indices, which include the effect through species richness; right: standardised effect sizes, at equal richness."

model <- tar_read(functional_model)
purrr::map_dfr(model, \(m) {
  m$summary.fixed[names(model_label), ] |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
    transmute(response = m$response, term, mean, lower = `0.045quant`, upper = `0.955quant`)
}) |>
  mutate(
    index = factor(
      if_else(grepl("fric", response), "Functional richness", "Functional dispersion"),
      c("Functional richness", "Functional dispersion")
    ),
    scale = factor(if_else(grepl("ses", response), "at equal richness (SES)", "raw"), c("raw", "at equal richness (SES)")),
    term = factor(model_label[term], rev(model_label)),
    effect = case_when(sign(lower) != sign(upper) ~ "Not credible", mean > 0 ~ "Positive", .default = "Negative")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, term, color = effect)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_effect) +
  facet_wrap(index ~ scale, scales = "free_x", labeller = \(x) label_value(x, multi_line = FALSE) |> lapply(\(l) sub(",", ":", l))) +
  labs(x = "Effect", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"))
```

**Results:**

- **Ammonium** does not change the raw functional richness, but lowers
  both indices at equal richness: species gained with ammonium are
  functionally redundant, those lost are distinct. A loss of functions
  hidden by a stable number of species.
- **Water temperature:** warmer rivers have more species and a higher raw
  functional diversity, but a lower functional diversity at equal
  richness.
- **Dams to the sea** lower the raw functional richness (fewer species, the
  migratory ones), and tend to lower the dispersion at equal richness.
- **Dam just upstream** slightly raises the functional richness at equal
  richness; the dam just downstream has no effect.

*To discuss:*

- Presence only: abundance-weighted indices (ASPE counts) would weight the
  dominant species, closer to the functions of the community.
- The null model keeps the frequency of each species; a null model drawing
  species from the regional pool would also test the filtering of which
  species reach a site.
- The trait choice matters; a sensitivity analysis dropping one group at a
  time would show which groups drive the results.

## Which functions become redundant?

Functional diversity falls with ammonium at equal richness: the species
gained are functionally similar to those already present, and those lost are
distinct. Three ways to look at this more finely.

### Winners and losers in the functional space

If ammonium favours "the same kind of species", the species it favours
should cluster in one region of the functional space, and those it
disfavours should lie at its edges. The distinctiveness of a species is its
mean functional distance to all other species, its uniqueness the distance to
its nearest neighbour [REF: Violle et al. 2017, doi:10.1016/j.tree.2017.02.002].

```{r winner-space}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "Species in the functional space (first two axes, left; axes 3 and 4, right), coloured by the effect of ammonium on their presence (D17, yearly model). Larger points: credible effects."

ammonium <- tar_read(species_pressure_response) |>
  filter(term == "ammonium") |>
  mutate(credible = sign(lower) == sign(upper))
winner <- species_coord |>
  inner_join(ammonium, by = "species")
effect_limit <- max(abs(winner$mean))
plot_winner <- function(x, y) {
  ggplot(winner, aes(.data[[x]], .data[[y]])) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey85", linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_point(data = anti_join(species_coord, winner, by = "species"), color = "grey80", size = 1.2) +
    geom_point(aes(fill = mean, size = credible), shape = 21, color = "grey30", stroke = 0.3) +
    ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
      aes(label = species), data = filter(winner, credible), size = 2.3, fontface = "italic",
      color = "grey25", max.overlaps = 20, segment.size = 0.2, seed = 1
    ) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#B2182B", mid = "grey95", high = "#2166AC", limits = c(-effect_limit, effect_limit),
      name = "Effect of ammonium\non presence"
    ) +
    scale_size_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 3, `FALSE` = 1.6), guide = "none") +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(x = sub("PC", "Axis ", x), y = sub("PC", "Axis ", y)) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")
}
patchwork::wrap_plots(plot_winner("PC1", "PC2"), plot_winner("PC3", "PC4"), guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

```{r distinctiveness}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Difference of response to each pressure per standard deviation of distinctiveness or uniqueness of the species (random-effects meta-regression as in D17, 91% credible interval). Negative: the more distinct species are more disfavoured."

tar_read(distinctiveness_response) |>
  mutate(
    term = factor(pressure_label[term], rev(pressure_label)),
    trait = c(distinctiveness_scaled = "Distinctiveness", uniqueness_scaled = "Uniqueness")[trait],
    effect = case_when(sign(lower) != sign(upper) ~ "Not credible", mean > 0 ~ "Positive", .default = "Negative")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, term, color = effect)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_effect) +
  facet_wrap(~trait) +
  labs(x = "Difference of response per sd of the trait", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "lines"))
```

**Results:**

- Ammonium splits the functional space along axis 2: the species it
  favours are open-water and still-water species (pikeperch, pike, rudd,
  carp, roach, perch, stickleback, mosquitofish), those it disfavours are
  bottom-dwellers (sculpin, brook lamprey, spined loach, minnow).
- The species favoured by ammonium are not functionally ordinary in the
  regional pool: their distinctiveness does not differ, and they are even
  slightly more unique. The loss of diversity is thus not a replacement of
  distinct species by ordinary ones, but a shift of the whole community
  towards one region of the functional space, where the species gained
  resemble each other.
- Warm water favours more unique species (e.g. catfish), as the lowland
  fauna is richer in distinct species.

### Which traits become redundant?

The functional diversity of each community is recomputed from the distance
of each trait group alone, with two indices on the distances between species
(target `pairwise_diversity`):

- **mean pairwise distance** (MPD): how different the species are on
  average;
- **mean nearest-neighbour distance** (MNND): how different each species is
  from its most similar neighbour in the community; it falls when the
  community holds near-copies of the same kind of species
  [REF: Swenson 2014, Functional and phylogenetic ecology in R, Springer].

Both are compared with the same null model (199 shuffles of species
traits) and modelled as above (targets `pairwise_ses`, `pairwise_model`).

```{r pairwise}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5.5
#| fig-cap: "Effect of dams and pressures on the functional diversity of each trait group at equal richness (standardised effect sizes; per standard deviation of the pressure, 91% credible interval)."

group_label <- c(
  All.traits = "All traits", Diet = "Diet", Habitat = "Habitat",
  Size.and.life.history = "Size and life history", Reproduction = "Reproduction", Morphology = "Morphology"
)
purrr::map_dfr(tar_read(pairwise_model), \(m) {
  m$summary.fixed[names(model_label), ] |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
    transmute(response = m$response, term, mean, lower = `0.045quant`, upper = `0.955quant`)
}) |>
  tidyr::separate_wider_delim(response, ".", names = c("index", "group"), too_many = "merge") |>
  mutate(
    index = factor(
      c(mpd_ses = "Mean pairwise distance", mnnd_ses = "Mean nearest-neighbour distance")[index],
      c("Mean pairwise distance", "Mean nearest-neighbour distance")
    ),
    group = factor(group_label[group], rev(group_label)),
    term = factor(model_label[term], model_label),
    effect = case_when(sign(lower) != sign(upper) ~ "Not credible", mean > 0 ~ "Positive", .default = "Negative")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, group, color = effect)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_effect) +
  facet_grid(index ~ term, labeller = labeller(term = label_wrap_gen(12), index = label_wrap_gen(18))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.1, 0.1)) +
  labs(x = "Effect at equal richness", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.spacing.x = unit(0.6, "lines"))
```

**Results:**

- **Ammonium** lowers the diversity of **size and life history** and of
  **diet** (and of morphology for the mean pairwise distance): communities
  at high ammonium hold species of similar size, longevity and fecundity,
  eating similar food. The nearest-neighbour distance in size and life
  history falls most: near-copies of the same kind of species.
- In contrast, ammonium raises the diversity of **reproduction** (and the
  habitat nearest-neighbour distance): the species gained spawn in more
  varied ways.
- **Water temperature** acts on other groups: warm communities are less
  diverse in habitat and morphology (fewer bottom-dwelling, elongated
  species), more diverse in diet and reproduction.
- **Dams to the sea** lower the diet diversity, probably through the loss
  of migratory species with distinct diets (eel, lampreys).

### In which direction?

Lower diversity at equal richness says that species become similar, not
towards which traits. The mean trait of the species present at each visit
(community mean, scaled) is modelled as the indices above (target
`community_trait_model`), for size, life history and diet. Diet breadth is
the Shannon diversity of the diet affinities of a species (high:
generalist). Temperature is shown for contrast.

```{r direction}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Change of the community mean trait (in standard deviations) per standard deviation of ammonium and of water temperature, 91% credible intervals."

trait_direction_label <- c(
  max_length = "Maximum length", longevity = "Longevity", age_maturity = "Age at maturity",
  fecundity = "Fecundity", diet_breadth = "Diet breadth", detritus = "Detritus",
  plants = "Plants", small_prey = "Small prey (< 1 mm)", medium_prey = "Medium prey (1-10 mm)",
  large_prey = "Large prey (> 10 mm)"
)
purrr::map_dfr(tar_read(community_trait_model), \(m) {
  m$summary.fixed[c("ammonium", "temperature"), ] |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
    transmute(term, trait = m$response, mean, lower = `0.045quant`, upper = `0.955quant`)
}) |>
  mutate(
    term = factor(pressure_label[term], pressure_label[c("ammonium", "temperature")]),
    trait = factor(trait_direction_label[trait], rev(trait_direction_label)),
    group = factor(
      if_else(trait %in% trait_direction_label[1:4], "Size and life history", "Diet"),
      c("Size and life history", "Diet")
    ),
    effect = case_when(sign(lower) != sign(upper) ~ "Not credible", mean > 0 ~ "Positive", .default = "Negative")
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean, trait, color = effect)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_effect) +
  facet_grid(group ~ term, scales = "free_y", space = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Change of the community mean trait", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "lines"), strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0))
```

**Results:**

- **Ammonium** shifts communities towards more fecund species with broader
  diets, eating more small prey and fewer large prey; size and longevity
  barely change on average.
- **Water temperature** shifts communities more strongly: towards larger,
  longer-lived, later-maturing and more fecund species with broader diets,
  eating more plants and fewer medium-sized invertebrates.

### Redundant species

A species is counted as redundant in a community if another species present
is a near-copy of it: their functional distance is among the 5% smallest
distances between the species of the pool (target `functional_redundancy`).
The number of redundant species, out of the number of species, is modelled
as the presence of species (binomial, same river position, sampling, site,
year and spatial effects), with the local dams, the logarithm of richness
(a near-copy is more likely in a richer community) and the pressure in
thirds of the visits: ammonium, with temperature controlled, and water
temperature, with ammonium controlled (target `redundancy_model`).
Phosphorus and oxygen are left out: they are part of the same pollution
syndrome as ammonium (correlations 0.73 and −0.49), so controlling for them
would remove part of the effect we look for.

```{r redundancy}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "Share of the species of a community that have a near-copy in it, per third of ammonium and of water temperature. Open circles: raw mean share. Filled: share adjusted for richness, river position, sampling, dams and the other pressure (91% credible interval), centred on the raw average of the thirds. Blue: credibly above the average of the thirds; red: below."

class_name <- c("Low", "Medium", "High")
redundancy_model <- tar_read(redundancy_model)
redundancy_raw <- purrr::map_dfr(redundancy_model, \(m) {
  add_pressure_class(tar_read(pressure_visit_wide), m$pressure, 3) |>
    select(operation_id, pressure_class) |>
    inner_join(
      tar_read(pressure_visit) |> filter(pressure == m$pressure) |> select(operation_id, raw = mean),
      by = "operation_id"
    ) |>
    inner_join(tar_read(functional_redundancy), by = "operation_id") |>
    summarise(
      range = if (m$pressure == "ammonium") {
        sprintf("%.2f to %.2f mg/L", 10^min(raw), 10^max(raw))
      } else {
        sprintf("%.1f to %.1f °C", min(raw), max(raw))
      },
      visits = n(),
      richness = mean(trials),
      share = mean(redundant / trials),
      .by = pressure_class
    ) |>
    arrange(pressure_class) |>
    mutate(pressure = m$pressure, class = factor(class_name, class_name))
})
redundancy_adjusted <- purrr::map_dfr(redundancy_model, \(m) {
  baseline <- mean(qlogis(redundancy_raw$share[redundancy_raw$pressure == m$pressure]))
  m$summary.lincomb.derived |>
    as_tibble(rownames = "class") |>
    transmute(
      pressure = m$pressure,
      class = factor(stringr::str_to_title(class), class_name),
      effect = case_when(`0.045quant` > 0 ~ "Positive", `0.955quant` < 0 ~ "Negative", .default = "Not credible"),
      mean = plogis(baseline + mean),
      lower = plogis(baseline + `0.045quant`),
      upper = plogis(baseline + `0.955quant`)
    )
})
redundancy_label <- bind_rows(
  filter(redundancy_raw, pressure == "ammonium", class == "High") |> transmute(pressure, class, y = share, label = "raw"),
  filter(redundancy_adjusted, pressure == "ammonium", class == "High") |> transmute(pressure, class, y = mean, label = "adjusted")
)
pressure_facet <- \(x) factor(pressure_label[x], pressure_label[c("ammonium", "temperature")])
ggplot(mutate(redundancy_adjusted, pressure = pressure_facet(pressure)), aes(class, mean)) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = share), data = mutate(redundancy_raw, pressure = pressure_facet(pressure)),
    shape = 21, size = 3, color = "grey40", fill = "white", stroke = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper, color = effect), linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(color = effect), size = 3) +
  geom_text(
    aes(y = y, label = label), data = mutate(redundancy_label, pressure = pressure_facet(pressure)),
    nudge_x = 0.15, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, color = "grey35"
  ) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_effect, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = c(0.6, 0.9))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1), expand = expansion(mult = 0.1)) +
  facet_wrap(~pressure) +
  labs(x = "Third of the pressure", y = "Species with a near-copy in the community") +
  theme(panel.spacing.x = unit(1.5, "lines"))
```

```{r redundancy-class}
redundancy_raw |>
  transmute(
    Pressure = pressure_label[pressure], Third = class, Range = range, Visits = visits,
    `Mean number of species` = round(richness, 1),
    `Species with a near-copy (raw)` = scales::percent(share, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

Which are the near-copies? For each pair of near-identical species, the
share of visits where both occur, in the low and in the high third of
ammonium (pairs occurring together in at least 2% of the visits of either
third).

```{r near-copy}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Near-identical species pairs: share of visits where both species occur, in the low (open) and high (filled) third of ammonium. Blue: more frequent at high ammonium; red: less frequent. Raw shares, not adjusted."

distance <- tar_read(functional_distance)$distance
threshold <- quantile(distance[upper.tri(distance)], 0.05)
pair_index <- which(upper.tri(distance) & distance <= threshold, arr.ind = TRUE)
ammonium_third <- add_pressure_class(tar_read(pressure_visit_wide), "ammonium", 3) |>
  select(operation_id, pressure_class) |>
  filter(pressure_class %in% c(1, 3))
third_visits <- count(ammonium_third, pressure_class, name = "visits")
third_presence <- tar_read(functional_presence) |>
  inner_join(ammonium_third, by = "operation_id")
near_copy <- tibble(
  species_1 = rownames(distance)[pair_index[, 1]],
  species_2 = rownames(distance)[pair_index[, 2]]
) |>
  purrr::pmap_dfr(\(species_1, species_2) {
    inner_join(
      filter(third_presence, species == species_1),
      filter(third_presence, species == species_2),
      by = c("operation_id", "pressure_class")
    ) |>
      count(pressure_class) |>
      right_join(third_visits, by = "pressure_class") |>
      transmute(pair = paste(species_1, "&", species_2), pressure_class, share = coalesce(n, 0L) / visits)
  }) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = pressure_class, values_from = share, names_prefix = "third_") |>
  filter(pmax(third_1, third_3) >= 0.02) |>
  mutate(
    direction = if_else(third_3 > third_1, "More frequent at high ammonium", "Less frequent at high ammonium"),
    pair = forcats::fct_reorder(pair, third_3 - third_1)
  )
ggplot(near_copy, aes(y = pair, color = direction)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = third_1, xend = third_3, yend = pair), linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = third_1), shape = 21, fill = "white", size = 2.3, stroke = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = third_3), size = 2.3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`More frequent at high ammonium` = "#2166AC", `Less frequent at high ammonium` = "#B2182B")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(1)) +
  labs(x = "Visits with both species", y = NULL, color = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic", size = 8), legend.position = "top")
```

Each third is compared with the average of the three thirds (sum-to-zero
coding), so that each gets its own credible interval; the adjusted shares
translate these differences, estimated on the logit scale, into
percentages around the raw average share.

**Results:**

- **Ammonium:** raw, the share of species with a near-copy rises from about
  a third in the low third to almost half in the medium and high thirds. At
  equal richness, river position, dams and temperature, part of this rise
  remains: the low third has credibly fewer redundant species than the
  average, the high third credibly more (about 39% against 41.5%).
- **The near-copies gained with ammonium** are pairs of still-water and
  tolerant species: perch and roach (together at 24% of the low-ammonium
  visits, 59% of the high ones), rudd and chub, stone loach and gudgeon,
  ruffe and perch, bleak and pumpkinseed, white bream and tench, crucian
  carp and tench. The pairs lost are flowing-water species: salmon and
  trout, minnow and spirlin, barbel and nase, trout and grayling.
- **Water temperature:** the raw rise is even steeper (28% to 50%), but it
  comes almost entirely from the higher richness of warm sites (14 species
  on average against 8 in cold sites): at equal richness, the share of
  redundant species barely differs between thirds (only the medium third is
  slightly above the average).
- So warm rivers hold more species and more near-copies, but no more than
  expected from their richness, whereas ammonium adds near-copies beyond
  richness.
- When phosphorus and oxygen are also controlled, the ammonium effect
  becomes smaller and not credible: redundancy follows the pollution
  syndrome as a whole rather than ammonium alone.

## Similarity between sites

Biotic homogenisation means that communities under a pressure become more
similar to each other across space
[REF: Olden et al. 2004, doi:10.1016/j.tree.2003.09.010]; it often shows as
a flatter distance-decay of dissimilarity: distant sites are less different
than they would be without the pressure
[REF: Olden & Rooney 2006, doi:10.1111/j.1466-822X.2006.00238.x]. We ask
whether sites under high ammonium are more similar to each other than sites
under low ammonium, and do the same for water temperature.

- **Classes.** One visit per site (the most recent); sites are split into
  thirds of the pressure (target `site_class`).
- **Pairs.** Only pairs of sites in the same third and less than 200 km
  apart. For each pair, the Sørensen dissimilarity is split into
  **turnover** (replacement of species) and **nestedness** (one community a
  subset of the other) [REF: Baselga 2010,
  doi:10.1111/j.1466-8238.2009.00490.x] (target `class_dissimilarity`).
- **Model.** Each dissimilarity is regressed on the class, the log distance
  between sites and their interaction (a distance-decay per class), with
  the mean and the difference of the two sites in river position (distance
  to the source, width, altitude, slope), dams to the sea and the other
  pressures (for ammonium, temperature only; for temperature, ammonium,
  phosphorus and oxygen), and whether they share a catchment. The second figure shows
  the predicted dissimilarity for each class at 100 km, with all these at
  their average, i.e. for pairs at the same position along the river and
  under the same other pressures. Pairs are not independent: the intervals come from 199
  bootstrap resamples of sites (target `class_dissimilarity_model`).
- **Dispersion.** The spread of the communities of each class
  around their centroid (multivariate dispersion,
  [REF: Anderson et al. 2006, doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2006.00926.x]), after
  removing the effect of river position and the other pressures (target
  `class_dispersion`). Homogenisation: lower dispersion.

```{r dispersion}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5
#| fig-cap: "Spread of the communities of each third of the pressure around their centroid, at the same river position and other pressures (91% bootstrap interval). Lower: more homogeneous."

class_label <- c(`1` = "Low", `2` = "Medium", `3` = "High")
colour_class <- c(Low = "#2166AC", Medium = "grey55", High = "#B2182B")
tar_read(class_dispersion) |>
  mutate(
    pressure = factor(pressure_label[pressure], pressure_label[c("ammonium", "temperature")]),
    class = factor(class_label[as.character(class)], class_label)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(class, dispersion, color = class)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_class, guide = "none") +
  facet_wrap(~pressure) +
  labs(x = "Third of the pressure", y = "Distance to class centroid")
```

```{r similarity}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Dissimilarity between sites of the same third of the pressure, and its two components, for sites 100 km apart at the same river position and other pressures (91% bootstrap interval)."

response_label <- c(sorensen = "Dissimilarity (Sørensen)", turnover = "Turnover", nestedness = "Nestedness")
tar_read(class_dissimilarity_model) |>
  filter(distance == 100) |>
  summarise(
    lower = quantile(predicted[replicate > 0], 0.045),
    upper = quantile(predicted[replicate > 0], 0.955),
    predicted = predicted[replicate == 0],
    .by = c(pressure, response, class)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    pressure = factor(pressure_label[pressure], pressure_label[c("ammonium", "temperature")]),
    response = factor(response_label[response], response_label),
    class = factor(class_label[as.character(class)], class_label)
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(class, predicted, color = class)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colour_class, guide = "none") +
  facet_grid(response ~ pressure, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Third of the pressure", y = "Predicted dissimilarity") +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0))
```

At equal environment, dissimilarity barely increases with distance
within 200 km (the river position, the pressures and the catchment
explain most of the differences between distant sites), so the
distance-decay curves are not shown.

**Results:**

- **Ammonium does not homogenise communities.** At the same river position,
  dams and temperature, sites of the high third are not more similar to
  each other than sites of the low third; they are slightly more different.
  Their differences come more from the replacement of species (higher
  turnover) and less from species-poor subsets (lower nestedness). The
  dispersion around the class centroid does not differ between low and
  high ammonium.
- **Water temperature homogenises communities.** Warm sites (medium and
  high thirds) are more similar to each other than cold sites, mostly
  through lower nestedness, and the dispersion around the centroid falls
  steadily from cold to warm sites, at the same river position.
- So ammonium reduces functional diversity within communities (more
  near-copies, previous sections) without making communities more alike
  across sites; warm water does make them more alike.

*To discuss:*

- One visit per site; using all visits would add the change of communities
  in time.
- The classes are thirds of the predicted pressure; within a class, sites
  still differ in pressure, especially in the highest third (long tail of
  ammonium).
- Taxonomic dissimilarity only; functional dissimilarity between sites
  would test functional homogenisation.

## Next steps

- Habitat specialisation (community specialisation index,
  [REF: Clavel et al. 2011, doi:10.1890/080216]): a first version
  (width x slope classes) ranked large-river species as specialists and
  trout as a generalist, because large rivers are rare and lumped in the
  ASPE sample and the thermal niche was left out; to redo with habitat
  classes on equal steps weighted by river network length, and separate
  structural, thermal and chemical specialisation.
- Abundance-weighted indices (ASPE counts), closer to the functions of the
  communities.
- Functional dissimilarity between sites, to test functional rather than
  taxonomic homogenisation.
